questions.q: Why does this lesson close Chapter 4 with a checklist rather than just a summary?
options: It's easy to think monitoring is "done" after setting things up, when some pieces were configured but never actually verified to work
A checklist is required by Azure and AWS before an environment can go live
A summary would take longer to read than a checklist
The chapter had no real content to summarize
questions.explain: The checklist is the difference between thinking monitoring is in place and confirming it's in place.

questions.q: What are the five points in this lesson's monitoring checklist?
options: Metrics configured, alerts configured, alerts tested, notification configured, and a dashboard created
Network deployed, compute deployed, storage deployed, backup configured, and documentation written
CPU, memory, disk, network, and security alerts, with no mention of notifications
Cost, performance, security, compliance, and availability reviews
questions.explain: These five points pull together the log destination, alert set, alert verification, notification routing, and dashboard from this chapter.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat "alerts configured" and "alerts tested" as two separate checklist items?
options: An alert rule that's never actually fired is an assumption, not a confirmed working alert — configured isn't the same as verified
Testing an alert automatically reconfigures it with better thresholds
Azure and AWS require a separate billing approval for testing
There is no real difference; the lesson lists them twice by mistake
questions.explain: Being syntactically valid is not the same as being verified — test-firing confirms the notification actually arrives end to end.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is an alert that fires into a notification channel nobody's watching functionally useless?
options: Because a fired alert still needs a real person subscribed on the receiving end to actually see and act on it
Because Azure automatically disables unwatched notification channels
Because unwatched channels cost more money than watched ones
Because it means the alert's threshold was set incorrectly
questions.explain: The alert and the notification are separate pieces — an alert firing into silence accomplishes nothing.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is still missing even after every checklist point is confirmed?
options: A way to actually get back online and recover data once monitoring tells you something is wrong — the subject of Chapter 5
Nothing; a completed checklist means the environment needs no further work
A second, duplicate monitoring system for redundancy
A larger compute instance to handle more alerts
questions.explain: Monitoring only tells you something went wrong; backup and disaster recovery, covered starting in Chapter 5, is what gets the environment back online.
